Is it not a fact that 75 per cent of the cattle from Alberta find their market in British Columbia to-day?

No, I would not say
that, not since the Underwood tariff came into effect, because I know that a large number of cattle from my district have recently been sold in the United States. I know that the Alberta hogs have found their market in Seattle and other Pacific coast points in the United States. I believe the same to be the case with oattle in that country. There is one thing to be said: even if the cattle of western Canada are sold in British Columbia, the fact that we have free entrance to the United States market has improved the price, to a very marked extent. I would point out that free wheat affects not only the farmer of western Canada but every man in business in that country. I do not know whether some of the western members who sit on the Government benches will deny this, but if I urn to go by the opinion which has been expressed to me by Conservative friends of mine since this matter has been discussed I would say that if the members in this House of both political parties from western Canada were to vote according to what they absolutely thought to be in the best interest of the farmers of western Canada, they would vote for free wheat and we would all stand together on that particular question. If any hon. members opposite deny that statement all well and good; I would like to have them do so, because it would be a valuable thing for us in their particular constituencies if they would go on record against free wheat. Free wheat is of importance not only to the farmers but to the men in the towns and cities of western Canada. During the crop season we in the West are all concerned about how the crop is coming along, what its prospects are. If we are having a dry season we are very much worried. The same thing is true about the price of wheat. Last year we had an exceptionally good crop but the price was exceptionally low, a discouraging feature to every man in business in that country, because he was looking to a profitable business from the farmers and hoped that with
a good crop there would be good prices and the farmer would be able to meet his obligations to the merchants and his purchasing power would be increased. But that was not the case. The price was low and the farmer was not able even to meet the debts he had contracted. In the face of that, the great agricultural implement industry of this country made demands upon the farmer that were never made in previous years, compelling him to pay up, and if he would not pay in the ordinary way putting him into court, seizing his property, taking everything from him in order to collect his indebtedness. That is one of the reasons why the agricultural implement industry is not gaining in popularity in western Canada.
The hon. member for Brandon to-day said, if I understood him rightly, that he believed that the Minister of Finance had an open mind on the question of free wheat, that he had not absolutely decided that free wheat would not be a good thing for this country. Then the member for Brandon proceeded to present some reasons to establish that free wheat would possibly not be a good thing for the farmer and he tried to so fix the mind of the Minister of Finance that there would be no possibility of free wheat. The [DOT]hon. member was frying to close the open miind of the Minister of Finance so that there would be no possibility of free wheat.
I want to deal for a few moments with the very important question of agricultural implements. As I had occasion to say in this House this session, during the campaign of 1911 gentlemen who appeared on the platform in opposition to myself in the constituency of Medicine Hat made the declaration that the chief fault with reciprocity was that it did not go far enough, especially on this item of agricultural implements; and they told the farmers that if the Conservative party were returned to power agricultural implements would be put on the free 'list. They made this statement throughout my riding. Now we find that they are not able to implement this promise, if I may be pardoned for the use of the word in that sense. They come down here and all they were able to get was a five per cent reduction on a certain agricultural implement. The Liberal provision in the reciprocity agreement covered nearly every implement which the farmer in western Canada uses. I say I believe that the men who spoke at that time were honest and believed that they would be able to convince the Conservative Government, if one came into existence, to provide free imple-

ments, but they have not been able to do so nor have the farmers of western Canada. But, on the other hand, the agricultural implement manufacturers of this country have been able to convince the Government that only a five per cent reduction is warranted.
I would like to read an extract from a western newspaper. It happens to be from my own paper published in the city of Lethbridge. It is not an editorial expression of opinion, but it is simply an interview given to one of the reporters by an agricultural implement man who does not use his own name-I presume he would be afraid of losing his position if he did- but he makes a very important statement. This article says that the agricultural implement men of the place were interviewed in order to get their views on the five per cent reduction in the duty on agricultural implements. The article continues:
The opinions were all very emphatic. One man said that the reduction could not help the farmer in the slightest degree. His reason was that all the binders sold in the west are manufactured in Canada anyway, with the exception of the John Deere, which sold for the same price as the others after the duty had been paid, namely $175.
The manufacturers in the East will pocket the advantage, said one man. Even if the price was lowered, it would not amount to more than five dollars on a binder. A farmer uses a hinder for an average of about five years-
I think that is a very small period of time in western Canada, but that is the length of time that this gentleman mentions as the life of a binder. Then the article continues:
-and if he saved $5 on his future purchases, that would mean a dollar a year, nothing that any farmer would write home about. What the farmers want, he continued, is free wheat, free food and free implements. If he had implements, the smaller manufactures in the United States would be permitted to invade this country, and they would make the larger concerns come down down to a point that would mean an advantage worth while to the farmer. With this, and free wheat, which would give the agriculturist a wider and better market, he might have financial benefits that would amount to something. The reduction on implements does not amount to the price of a good square meal to the farmer.
That is an expression of opinion from western Canada, and it comes from one of the agricultural implement men. In this connection I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) to a statement which has been made to me. I cannot guarantee that it is correct because I have been away from the West for some time, but the statement is that within the last three or four months
[Mr. Buchanan, j
the price of binders and mowers in western Canada has been increased sufficiently to cover any reduction which might be made in the duty on agricultural implements. That statement was made to me by a gentleman in my own city, and if it is correct it is worthy of investigation. I cannot guarantee that it is correct, but I simply make the statement as it was made to me.
Will the hon. gentleman repeat that statement?

The statement that was made to me was that the price of binders and mowers had been increased about $5 within the last three or four months. This gentleman who wrote to me, since the announcement of the reduction in the duty, intimated that the agricultural implement manufacturers must have been figuring on a reduction in the duty, and so they put up the price. I cannot guarantee the accuracy of that statement, but the statement was made by a responsible business man.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be quite impossible that that could be done, for the reason that-I make the statement, without any equivocation or reserve-nobody could be aware of the action of the Government in the matter, and I do not believe the statement is correct.

I would not want to say that the manufacturers were advised that there was any possibility of a reduction, but I think that from the discussion which had been taking place in this country during the last few months they might have imagined that something was going to happen, and they certainly could have imagined that something was going to happen if the party on this side of the House had anything to do with the changes in the tariff. I do not say that they knew actually that a five per cent reduction, or any reduction, was to be made, but if the statement that they have increased the price over that for which they had been selling these binders in western Canada is correct, it is worthy of investigation at any rate. I had the opportunity of making a speech on this question before in the House, and I do not intend to make any further remarks on this particular subject.
I want, however, to offer some observations on the question of immigration. This is an important question to the people of western Canada. We are all anxious that our country should develop as rapidly as

possible. My own conclusion is that, outside of the people who have been coming in and taking up homesteads, there has been practically no movement to the West of the class of farmers who might be expected to invest in farm lands. A great many people who went into western Canada as homesteaders simply went in to prove up, get the land and then move away. We have in many cases vacant homesteads, and naturally there has been a decrease of population in that regard. I do not know whether that is the case in all districts or not, but I know that is the case in many parts of Alberta. We have not been bringing into western Canada as we should have done men to go on the land and till the soil. Western Canada is out of the stage of sensational development by means of real estate speculation, which has aroused the people to a realization of the possibilities of their respective cities. They have spent a great deal of money in development. I say that population practically will be stationary until there is a very rapid increase in our rural population. I would like to see more people going into that country and settling on the land. They are not coming in to purchase farm lands as they were a few years ago. I do not know whether there is any slackening of the efforts to bring settlers from the United States or not, but there certainly has not been the movement of United States settlers to southern Alberta that there was a few years ago: In that particular part of the country the United States settler is an ideal settler. He comes from states which are very similar in climate and agricultural conditions to Southern Alberta, and he generally makes a success of agriculture. I hope that the efforts to bring farmers in from the United States will continue, and that the class of immigrants that we are bringing from across the sea will be a class of people who will go on the farms. We should now make every effort to get people on the land. That should be the main object of this Government if it wants development to continue in western Canada, population to increase and the resources of the country to yield what it is possible for them to yield.
What is the cause of men leaving the land in Alberta ?
Land has been vacated by what are known as professional homesteaders.
Brought in by the former Government ?

There has also been a movement of actual farmers of western Canada according to the conditions there. I would not say how great that movement is, but I have in my desk a clipping from a newspaper published in my district showing that from that particular district there has been a very large movement of farmers.
Where did they go ?
The statement was made that some went back to the United States and some to Ontario.

I think I explained that a couple of weeks ago when I stated that the land laws of the state of Montana had been made very much more generous recently, that the United States Government now are giving homesteads of 320 acres where they used to give them of 160 acres, and that they are allowing people to qualify for patents in three years, while heretofore they demanded five years. Of course, their lands are inferior to ours, but at the same time this has a very great influence in attracting settlement in that direction.

My argument is that we should bend all our efforts to get people into the West who will become permanent settlers on the land. One of the reasons for the movement of population out of certain parts of my constituency is to be found in the fact that railroads have promised that they will build lines within a few years into those districts, but notwithstanding that many settlers have been living on their homesteads for five years there is no sign of a railroad in their neighbourhood yet, and they have become discouraged and have left the country. The Government, in my opinion, should insist upon the more speedy construction of branch lines into districts which are well settled. I cannot understand why railroads will build branch lines into unsettled parts of the country, when there are well settled districts in which railroads are absolutely needed. The Government should get behind these railroad companies with a big stick and make them build these branch lines, according to their promises, so as to keep the people in the country, and thus remove a great deal of discontent. In my own district, the Canadian Northern Railway Company has followed this practice of promising to build branch lines into certain districts, and when the settlers go in they do not build them.
jitjiia

I represent a district where railroads are absolutely needed, and where the farmers, in many cases, are settled from fifty to seventy miles from railroad facilities. I am prepared to stake my political future on the declaration that I would not tender any assistance whatever to the Canadian Northern Railway Company until Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann shall get rid of their other interests, their street railways, and their electric power companies, and their coal mines on the Pacific coast, and their other interests throughout Canada and in foreign countries, and save the Canadian Northern railway with their own resources. I may be radical in this respect, hut I believe I have my constituents back of me when I say, that if the Canadian Northern railway cannot be saved by Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann themselves then the people of Canada, who up to the present have really built that road, should take it over and operate it themselves. And, while we probably have not made a success of operating the only Government-owned road we have in this country, still I think we might do much worse than to take over the Canadian Northern railway, rather than to hand over a guarantee of bonds or any other assistance to the men who are now at the head of that undertaking. These gentlemen have been assisted by every province in this Confederation; they have been assisted by the Dominion Government, and they would not be so far advanced as they are to-day with their lines were it not that the people of Canada have rendered them liberal assistance. If these gentlemen cannot finish that railroad system and put it in such a position as to operate it successfully, I say the people of Canada should safeguard themselves and take the road into their own possession.
I have devoted my remarks chiefly to questions affecting western Canada, and I conclude by saying that I dislike very much to hear members in this House give expression to the idea that western Canada is always complaining, and always has a grievance. That is not the kind of talk that will make western Canada more friendly to eastern Canada. We in the West have grievances which must be remedied before we are a contented people, and I want to say for the people of western Canada that they are just .as anxious for a united Canada, and just as anxious for a prosperous and progressive eastern Canada, as they are for a prosperous and progressive western Canada. . But they will continue to insist that

their grievances, more especially with respect to tariff matters, shall be remedied, and once these grievances are remedied you would have happy and contended farmers on the prairies of the West.
I appeal to members on both sides of this House to unite in a statesman-like effort to meet the needs of western Canada. If western Canada is to grow and to make progress, it must be looked to with a sympathetic eye by whatever Government may be in power. I repeat what I have often said, that Canada will not be prosperous and progressive unless we place on the lands of western Canada settlers who will till the soil and produce that wealth which will enable them to purchase the output of the industries of eastern Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I come from one of the principal dairying centres in the province of Ontario, in which is held the largest weekly market for dairying product that there is to be found in Canada, and I therefore feel it incumbent on me, when we are discussing tariff matters, to speak on behalf of the dairying industry. I shall address the House from the viewpoint of a dairy man and a business man of the province of Ontario. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) spoke of the policy of the Liberal Government. Having been a close student of the different policies introduced by the late Government, I cannot for the life of me understand which of the Liberal policies the hon. gentleman alluded to, because the Liberal party has had so many policies that I must admit I have not been sufficiently alert to have kept track of them. Perhaps the hon. gentleman referred to the Liberal policy of giving away the resources of this country to their friends, in the shape of water-powers, town-sites, timber limits and other things. The right hon. leader of the Opposition has stated on more than one occasion in this House that he is not a business man, and therefore, I presume, he will not be able to appreciate the remarks which I make from a business man's standpoint.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance upon his Budget Speech. He deserves the congratulations of the people of Canada for his business-like attitude on tariff questions, and for the executive ability he displayed in that financial statement. I think I can safely say that during the regime of the Laurier Administration no Minister of

Finance ever delivered such a masterly Budget Speech, or one so calculated to contribute to the development and prosperity of our country.
The hon. Minister of Finance referred to the money stringency of 1907-08, which is not so long ago but we can all distincly remember it. Yet in the face of that stringency, Sir Wilfrid Laurier appealed to the people to return him at the head of the Government so. that he could finish his work. The people did so, and now they are paying the penalty. The money stringency has been world wide. It has affected not only Canada, but the great nation to the south of us, and all European countries. I am proud to say, however, that the people of Canada have felt it as little as any other nation in the world. I live right on the international boundary line; and from my house, I can see what is happening across the line. How de we find conditions there at the present time? How are railway men affected there? The New York Central railway, which is not a transcontinental line by any means, has discharged no less than 25,000 employees since February, 1914. Have we had a similar experience in Canada? No; our railway men say they have no particular complaint to make. Take the situation as it exists in New York today. How many hundred thousand men are there out of employment in that city? Why does that bread-line exist in New York at the corner of 35th street and Fifth avenue, where the hungry people are fed from midnight until two o'clock every night by that great organization known as the Christian Herald Newspaper Company? That is surely sufficient to cause alarm. What would our hon. friends opposite say if the cities of Ottawa and Montreal were running a bread-line at that hour of the night? In New York you can get men furnished by that Christian organization for practically their food and clothes; but when you want a man in Canada to go on a farm, he asks from $45 to $$50 a month. That is sufficient to show the difference between conditions in Canada and conditions in the United States at the present time.
I have listened, most earnestly to the arguments brought forward in favour of free food. I would like to ask the right hon. the leader of the Opposition: Where is this free food to be found? Where is it to come from? Is Canada not one of the greatest producing nations in the world? Are we not proud of the position which the agriculturists of this country occupy today? We are, and the farmers of this coun-169
try, by obtaining high prices, are only coming into their own, and I hope they will continue to get those high prices for the next twenty-five years. They are only now beginning to realize what it is to have a home market at their own door. That is the best market for the products of the farm. The field crops of Canada last year reached the enormous sum of $553,000,000. Where was this great crop consumed? Eighty per cent of the total crop of Canada was consumed in her own markets. The farmer deserves the same amount of protee-9 p.m. tion as the manufacturer, the artisan, the mechanic and the labourer. Ontario, with its 2,500,000 people, produced no -less than 40 per cent of the total agricultural products of Canada during 1913. Ontario had over 9,500,000 acres of field crops in 1911. Ontario has nearly 300,000 acres in orchards, vineyards and small fruits. I would ask the right hon. leader of the Opposition: what did it mean to the producer of those fruits to have free fruit coming into Canada? The people in the United States -are about thirty days ahead of us in the production of the berry crop. Would my right hon. friend rob the farmers.of the profit of producing those berries for the tables of the artisans and mechanics in the cities? The farmers deserve the greatest consideration that can possibly be afforded them. We are all proud of our farmers, because they are the bone and sinew of the country 'and they have made Canada what dt is to-day.
The farmers of Ontario alone have a working capital invested of $1,216,864,990; but they have received in the legislature the least consideration of any class of people that has any such investment in this country. I am prepared to give to the .farmers of Ontario and Quebec their full share of the credit due them for what they have done to make Canada known in the markets of the world. The pioneer farmers who came into this country, possibly a hundred years ago, did as much to roll back the curtain of civilization to the rest of the world and to advertise Canada as any class of people that we have in Canada to-day.
I have listened with great interest to the stories of hardship of the prairie farmers, told .by hon. members from the West. If you compare the condition of the prairie farmer with that of the pioneer who came into this country .a hundred years ago, as my grandfather did, who went fifty miles to a mill with a bushel of wheat across his horse's back, along a blazed road, and if you think of the advantages possessed by the western farmer, those hardships pale

into a shadow. The pioneers of Canada have done something to which we can all point with the finger of pride. The farmers of Ontario and Quebec have been what we might term the pioneers or the pathfinders of the great West. Going through my constituency, I often hear people regretting that the young men and the young women, the pride of our country, are now going out to the great western provinces to make their homes; but I am pleased to think that there are so many of the best young men and women of Ontario and Quebec in the West, and I am sure they will see that the interests of that country are properly conserved. During a trip I made through the western provinces last autumn, I was told on many occasions that the farmers who came from the older provinces of the Dominion of Canada were the best settlers there. We have heard a great deal about the boys leaving the farm. Well, up to the present time of high prices, the boys on the farm had very little to encourage them to stay there, and the fault in that case, I think, can be laid at the door of the previous Government. The provincial Government in Ontario to-day by the development of its HydTo-Eleetric scheme, is doing more to keep the young men on the farm than has *been done by any other government in this country within the past fifty years. If young men leave the farm because they cannot make ends meet what is the reason of that condition? The shortage of help. Why has Ontario received so little consideration in the past in her immigration policy? Simply because the late Government of this Dominion wanted the settlers to go to the West. But to-day the province of Ontario is getting her full share of farm labour, and I expect to see the results of that immigration showing in the increased products of our farms. There is only one way that I know of to reduce the high cost of living in this country, and that is to populate the rural districts. We have too many consumers and not enough producers. That is the secret of the situation. But if this policy of free food introduced by the leader of the Opposition is to sweep away the protection afforded our farmers, what encouragement, I ask you, Sir, would there be for young men to take up farming in the province of Ontario?
The hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) spoke of the dairy industry. I have been engaged in that calling for the past thirty-five years, so when I speak of the dairy industry, I take the liberty of believing that I speak of something which I understand. Our dairying industry has been

developed during the past thirty-five years. Our beginnings, as is usual with beginnings, were small, but the product of the dairy industry of Canada for the year 1913 was estimated at the large sum of $121,000,000. Canada's dairy exports last year amounted to $21,714,153, those exports consisting almost entirely of cheese. The hon. member for Huntingdon spoke of the [advantages of shipping milk and cream. But let me say to the members of the House-'and I know whereof I speak-that the man who ships milk and cream off Ms farm, and has nothing coming back to feed his hogs and calves, is minting his land. He is like the man who is selling hay-how long can he continue to raise a hay crop? Go into the northern part of the state of New York and find there the farmers who have been supplying New York city with milk, and you will find that these are the people who are coming over to Ontario and buying our young cattle to build up their dairies. Their old cows 'are milked out, and they must do something to increase their herds. I have farmers in my constituency who last year raised a calf for every cow they milked and sold those calves for $25 apiece. But that was another mistake. Instead of selling that young stock, they should have sold the finished 'article, the food product, for in that way they would have doubled their income in a short time.
We have heard a good deal about the cattle exported to the United States during October and November after the new Wilson tariff came into effect. What do these cattle consist of? To a large extent of young stock, one-year olds and two-year olds. That is a mistake that our farmers made. They shipped as high as thirty-five or forty in one ear,, and we saw carload after carload going out of our country. To-day many farmers regret that they sold that stock, for they could sell it in the home market to-day, in Saskatchewan or British Columbia, for more money.
The hon. membeir for Huntingdon referred to the ' Jingoes of Ontario.' Well, I have lived ini Ontario all my life, and 1 do not know the meaning of his word. But I do know wbat caused- the wonderful upset in the calculations of hon. gentlemen opposite on the 21st of September, 1911. It was not because of jingoes, but because the people of Ontario were too independent ever to become 'an adjunct.' That speech which Hon. Champ Clark made about the Stars and

Stripes floating from ocean to ocean and from the pole to the gnlf is what made the ' jingoes,' and when the same question comes up again, you will find the people of Canada just as independent and just as loyal as they were on that 21st day of September.
Speaking further of the cattle export, I have taken some figures from the Monetary Times, which will be regarded as an authority anywhere in Canada. There were sold from Alberta last year, $10,000,000 worth of cattle. Of this $5,000,000 went to British Columbia, $4,500,000 worth to Winnipeg and Calgary for local consumption, and $500,000 worth to the United States. I visited that abattoir in Calgary last summer and observed with great interest the way in which they handled that stock. I saw them load carload after carload for British Columbia and Winnipeg, but while I was there they did not load one carload of cattle, sheep or hogs for the United States. What is the trouble to-day with the United States markets for cattle, when we see the western cattle from Saskatchewan and Alberta being offered on the Toronto and Montreal markets? Western cattle to-day control the Montreal market. It must be that the home market offers the producers and drovers of western Canada more than does the United States market.
Now, I desire to refer briefly to the bacon and hog products of Canada. I would like some hon. gentleman opposite to tell me what it will mean to the dairymen of this country to have free wheat. Our dairymen are depending, on the offal, that is, the bran, shorts and low-grade flour to feed hogs for the production of pork and bacon. During the past 25 years this country has built up a reputation second to none in the world for the quality of the bacon and cured meats that it manufactures and exports. When I was in British Columbia last year, I went with a drover from Grand Forks into the state of Washington, and I saw him purchase dressed hogs in that state for $10 a hundredweight, paying upon them 3 cents per lb. duty, and taking them to his customers, the miners and smelt workers of Grand Forks. Yet the right hon. leader of the Opposition wishes to wipe out, with one stroke of the pen, this great industry which has been built up by our farmers. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that without protection the hog-producers and bacon-curers of this country would be put out of business.
What would free wheat mean to the 169J
milling industry ? It would simply drive it out of business. It has been our proud boast in the past that the people of Canada control more natural resources than tbe people of any other country on the continent. We have to-day lumber for the manufacture of barrels, we have our cotton mills for the manufacture of flour bags, and we are employing a large amount of capital in the milling industry. In the face	of	these	considerations, free
food and free wheat would simply drive the milling industry out of Canada. The mills in a short time would be built to the south of the line, where the-millers could get low-grade wheat to mix with the high	standard wheat weproduce in Canada. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, for one moment that the people of the United States require our wheat for domestic use? No; they simply need a certain percentage of the No. 1 hard wheat which we produce in Canada to grade up their low standard wheat in order to make a better class of flour to compete with the Canadian millers in the markets across the seas. The great milling concerns of Minneapolis and Buffalo came into the Canadian market last autumn and bought 10,000,000 bushels of wheat, upon which they paid duty. Do you think that if they could have obtained the same high-grade wheat in the south they would have come over here and taken Canadian wheat? No, not for one moment. I do not think any sane man would believe such a thing.
What would it mean to the dwellers in the city, for whom our friends across the floor of this House have so much sympathy, if we were to take any step which would increase the price of bran and shorts say $3 a ton? It would mean that we would have to pay 12i instead of 8 or 9 cents a quart for milk with which to feed the children of this country. That is another consideration which our friends opposite have apparently overlooked. One thing is certain: the producers of milk must receive some reward for their labour, and if you increase the cost of feed you must expect the producer of milk to increase the price of the product.
I have tried to explain in a fair and reasonable manner just how this great industry would be effected by free wheat. The United States is the third largest exporter of wheat to the British market, and for every bushel of wheat they would take from Canada it is quite natural to suppose that they would have one bushel of American

wheat to export to Great Britain. We are all proud of the position which we occupy as exporters; why should we try to injure the position which we now hold and are so proud of? With free wheat, and with our wheat going to the south instead of to the east and west, we would be advertising the United States as the greatest producer of wheat in the world. If the American miller wishes to secure Canadian wheat in bond for grinding purposes, it costs him only one-tenth of a cent per bushel, and he has the bran, shorts and offal in his own country. With that small increase in cost they claim that they can compete with the Canadian miller in the foreign markets. But I do think the millers of the United States are quite capable of guarding their own interests. It is not in the interests of either the millers or the producers of Canada that the people of the United States are so anxious to have our No. 1 northern hard wheat entered into the United States free of duty. This is not a party question; it is a great national question and I think it is time that our friends across the floor of this House began to realize that fact. If we were to listen to the offers that our friends have been in the habit of making., occasionally to catch voters throughout the country, we would be pursuing the same policy that they have been pursuing for a great length of time. The right hon. leader of the Opposition is beginning to realize that the farmers of this country have some cause to doubt the value of these apparently favourable proposals that he is continually making to them. By appealing to the artisan, the mechanic and the labourer and telling them that the high cost of living is depressing them, he may possibly catch their votes and the votes of the western farmers. But I would like hon. gentlemen opposite to explain where they are going to get this cheap food which is to be brought into Canada. What is wanted in Canada is more wheat to be ground in this country, thereby increasing the production of the farmers along dairying lines, along meat lines and in many other ways. By doing this we will be doing our share towards lowering the high cost of living.
The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) said last night that he for one would, if it were necessary for this Government to do so, approve the establishing of a line of ocean vessels that would govern the export rates on flour and wheat. I would do all in my power to further a policy of that kind if it were necessary in
	.
the interests of the western farmer. By so doing I think we would be doing more for the western farmer than we would be doing if we were to take the duty off wheat and let it come into this country free.
Another matter in respect of which I wish to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance is that in his Budget he did better in regard to agricultural implements than hon. gentlemen opposite did in their reciprocity pact. Under the reciprocity proposal the duty on these implements was to be fifteen per cent, but the hon. Minister of Finance has cut the duty on binders, mowers, harvesters and reapers to twelve and one-half per cent. For this he should receive the congratulations of the farming community.
A word about this pact known as reciprocity and larger markets. We were told by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mil. 'Mr. Speaker, I cannot recall an occasion upon which I did myself the honour to take part in a Budget speech in this House, and I think I can therefore say that this will be my maiden speech on that shbject. I would not participate in this discussion were it not for the fact that I think the time has arrived in Canada for those who have convictions to give expression to their vie,ws. The time has come, and I think I am" not extravagant in stating that the struggle has begun. History tells us that there have been cycles of stress and struggle between the classes in every age and every land. Two thousand years ago there was such a struggle and it was a struggle of the
classes against the masses. Down through the history of every age these struggles have been recorded; and while the contestants have had different names the struggle has been the same. We have had it in Canada. They are having a struggle to-day in Great Britain. There it' has been a contest between the aristocracy and the democracy. In Canada, in the early days, there was a struggle of the people against the family compact. It was the fight for responsible government, and in every one of the four original provinces of this Dominion that struggle went on. It is upon us to-day in a different farm. It is a struggle between the interests and the great mass of the people. It is all very well for ns to laugh and say that there is no power that controls in Canada to-day. We know that it is true that even in the matter of legislation, as every hon. member has realized in his experience, there are interests that control and influence in a mighty degree, almost in a paramount degree in Canada, even in this Parliament. We see occasionally immense delegations travelling to Ottawa, interviewing the Government. They are heard with consideration, with courtesy and with respect. But, Sir, these delegations are powerless to influence the currents of legislation and governmental action. We saw here the other day, on the floors of this Parliament, an immense delegation with respect to a great transportation scheme. Were they misled? Did they return to their homes with the thought that they had made an impression upon the Government or even upon Parliament? If they did they deceived themselves because we know that the question is subject to the control and influence-perhaps I should not use the word dictation-of certain interests that are considered rival interests. If it comes, to a struggle then I wish in no uncertain way to assert my views, to pronounce myself and to co-operate, as I believe, with the great masses against the classes in Canada.
It is very easy to be placed on the wrong trail and follow it until it leads away from the right one. I think that has happened in Canada. The trouble is that we have not cared to call things by their proper names. Ambition is what we choose to term that insensate lust for material prosperity which is the maggot at the heart of such success. Protection is the soil on which corruption grows. Our whole body politic is menaced, mentally, socially and morally -politically speaking-by corruption. It is the gathered force, the concentrated intensity of all the accumulated greed for power
