tariff all the time.

It is very strange
that that same protective tariff, as my hon. friend calls it, could not be made to work when controlled by his party and that, when it came under the control of the Liberal party, it was a successful tariff. If it was a protective tariff, let me ask my hon friend why it was that in 1908 the present right hon. leader of the Government, from his place on this side of the House, moved a resolution in favour of adequate protection? If we had under the Liberal regime in 1908 a protective tariff that was adequate, why was it necessary for my right hon. friend to ask this Parliament to pass a motion m favour of adequate protection?
Simply a phrase.

I find that my hon.
friend indulges in too many phrases, meaningless though they may be.
Simply a pretext.
Yes, there have been too many pretexts by my hon. friend s party when in opposition, and there are more pretexts to-day.

There were more labour disturbances during the regime of my hon. friends opposite in 1906 and 1907 than there have been since. Nobody but the

Opposition is complaining in the country to-day.
My hon. friend can console himself with that thought. He will have great difficulty in convincing the people on that point.
It will be quite easy.

My hon. friend in stating to the House that the word ' adequate ' was merely a pretext is certainly giving an illustration of the meaning of politics as it baa been defined by one very eminent authority. That definition of protection is as follows:
Politics in practice too often means all for party, nothing- for the people; all for policy, nothing for principle; all for office, nothing for honour; all for power, nothing for progress.
Politics 'is the 'science of exigencies with this Government. My hon. friend admits on behalf of his party that that was the kind of politics in which he and his
10 p.m. friends were indulging on that occasion. I do not wish, however, to travel from the point. If we have had the National Policy during all these years, why is it that my hon. friends opposite took this action to have it changed? Why was it that Sir Charles Tupper, at the very inception of the policy characterized it as a tariff that would do incalculable injury to Canada? It burst in a measure the shackles which bound the trade of Canada. By reason of placing on the free list so many articles which entered into the industrial life of Canada, it enabled manufacturing interests to advance and to prosper. It gave employment to the many thousands who were obliged to be the wage earners of the country, and it gave an impetus to our agricultural interests, to our immigration that has certainly never been paralleled in the history of Canada. My hon. friend knows that taxing is an easy business; but, as Edmund Burke once said: Taxing is an easy business :
Any projector can contrive new impositions; any bungler can add to the old; but is it altogether wise to have no other bounds to your impositions than the patience of those who are to bear them?
The idea put forward in the motion relating to adequate protection was one which meant placing additional burdens upon the people of the country. The reason it was not accepted by this House and that it was not favoured by the people of the country at the time was because 
there was an abounding prosperity. Trade was advancing by leaps and bounds. In every branch of industry in every department of commercial activity, there was action, success and reward. The people did not approve of any suggestion that meant what is 130 easy of accomplishment unden- certain circumstances, the imposition of additional taxation. It is not wise to have your imposts up to the limit df the patience of those who bear the burdens. I call attention to the fact that the tariff of 1879 admitted certain articles free upon action to be taken by the Congress of the United States. That clause of the tariff of 1879 is already upon ' Hansard ' and I will not repeat it. I merely say that the Finance Minister, while he has been very attentive to the interests of the manufacturers and to certain other interests, had not a word . to say in all bis splendid address about the burdens of the masses or the increased cost of living. He was silent on that subject-there was not a word with respect to the burdens which the people to-day are bearing. It is all very well far us to try to ignore as of very little importance the fact that the cost of living is increasing month by month, as official figures prove. It is true, this increase in the cost of living has taken place in all countries, but that increase is not so great in Great Britain as in protectionist countries, and nowhere has that increase been so great as in Canada.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say: You were content under the tariff which existed .when you were in power, but now because you are .in -Opposition you want it changed. We all realize that time brings changes, that new conditions arise year by year and month by month. When the tariff was *amended in 1907, trusts amd combines were not in evidence to the extent they are today. I am one of those who at times have felt that the Liberal party has not advanced as it should have advanced with respect to that question. I am free to admit that. But I believe that the Liberal party stands to-day ready to advance, and it is because of that that I am ready to pat them on the back. The trusts land combines have grown in a remarkable degree even since the introduction of the Fielding taa-ifi in 1897. Changes 'and modifications were made in that tariff, the greatest in 1907, and had the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier succeeded at the polls in 1911, still greater

changes would, have been made. But these trusts -and combines have grown to such enormous proportions that the people realize their existence and power.
Can the hon. gentleman name some of them?

I could name many. I have a list of them somewhere here, but it is hardly worth while to read it. These trusts are growing year by year; there is the coal trust, the steel trust, the millers' trust, the canners' trust-there is a trust in almost every direction. I believe that protective tariffs stimulate the growth of trusts in Canada. The very object of protective tariffs is to protect the industries of the country. And for a time it may succeed, while competition can be maintained. But the time comes when these men are not content merely with an adequate profit; their greed-for they are but human-urges them forward to seek more and more at the expense of the consumer. The time has come in Canada, in my judgment, when some change should be made to prevent the coming together of these interests. If the tariff of to-day helps these trusts and combines to wring undue profits out of the people, then, though as a Liberal I for years supported thek tariff, I say, for one, let us eliminate from the tariff every vestige of protection.
The hon. gentleman is an out-and-out free trader.

I am an out-and-out free trader, and I wish circumstances permitted the adoption of free trade. I am to-day where I have always been. This Canadian Confederation was launched on the basis of indirect taxation; I quite understand that, and we have continued that policy. But if you could change the policy of indirect taxation and adopt a direct tax, then indeed you could have free trade. Speaking for myself, if .a plan were proposed which would actually bring that about, I would hold up both hands for it.
The Minister of Finance dealt with the steel industry, and took some action with respect to agricultural implements. There is one subject to which I invited his attention a short time ago which he has apparently ignored. The agriculturists of eastern Canada are not interested so much in the question of agricultural implements as presented to this Parliament as they are interested in another phase of the queetion
of free raw materials for their production. I asked the Minister of Finance some few weeks ago to consider the question of fertilizers and basic slag. At that time I brought to his notice and to the notice of the House the conditions in eastern Canada with respect to basic slag and its use as a fertilizer. I believe in the principle of free agricultural implements for the agriculturist because they are the agriculturist's raw material, and fertilizers should be made free because they are the raw material which assists him in producing his products. I do not wish to repeat the argument that I attempted to bring before the House on that occasion, but I want to bring to your notice, Sir, and to the notice of the minister that in contrast with the treatment accorded by the Government to the big interests, the organized farmers have not been treated with that respect which is their due. A single manufacturer can have the duty on a certain article increased; as instance the case of this gentleman from Cape Breton who, in secret, secured by a stroke of the pen an order of the Customs Board imposing a duty upon basic slag, a fertilizer in very general use by the agriculturists and horticulturists of the eastern provinces. I have here a letter from a gentleman whom I do not personally know, but who is, I think, the secretary of the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers' Association. In a letter addressed to me in March of this year, he said, among other things:
I thought I would write you direct to place before you some facts as to how -this ruling of the customs board will effect the fruit growers of the Annapolis valley.
Within recent years basic slag has become one of the most important fertilizers in the growing of apples. The only plant food it contains is phosphoric acid, of which it has from twelve to fourteen per cent available, but in addition to this it contains from forty to sixty per cent of lime, and lime while not a direct fertilizer has a great effect on the dormant plant food in the soil, rendering it more available. On account of this lime slag as a source of phosphoric acid is much superior to and is rapidly taking the place of acid phosphate in orchards, and in growing grain and hay crops. When apple growing on a commercial scale was first started in this valley, the fruit-growers depended chiefly on their stables for fertilizer, and a man was discouraged from raising more orchard than he could manure in that way. Within the last fifteen years, however, mixed farming has declined, and the farmer who found himself with too many irons in the fire, has stood by the orchard and dropped the less profitable and less laborious stock farming, but in doing this he finds he has to look elsewhere for plant food to feed his trees, and thousands of tons of commercial fertilizer

are imported every spring at a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
With the great increase in apple orchards all over America we must expect in a few years a vastly increased production, and optimistic as I would like to feel, it forced upon me, however, in the light of this fact that the country that will survive in this apple-growing competition, is the country that can produce them the cheapest. Now Nova Scotia with her cheap lands, her nearness to the markets of the world, her water transportation, is wonderfully situated in this respect, but anything like unfair prices on fertilizers and spraying materials, places a serious handicap on these advantages.
In the Annapolis valley we virtually manufacture apples and use commercial fertilizers as a raw material. Why siiould we not be placed on the same basis as other manufacturers and have our raw material free? It is vastly more important to build up the business of fruit-growing in Nova Scotia than it is the business of manufacturing fertilizers. The Cross Fertilizer Company in Sydney have a complete monopoly, as slag for fertilizer is not made anywhere else in Canada. Slag, as every one knows, is a by-product in the manufacture of steel, and until two years ago was thrown into the harbour at Sydney as utterly worthless. The process of grinding is inexpensive, and everything above the cost of grinding is clear profit.
I will leave to any one's common sense the fairness of taxing the fruit growers of this valley to put an extra profit in the pocket of the stockholders of the Cross Fertilizer Company. On account of our wet, cold springs, our orchards are especially susceptible to the disease of apple scab or black spot. To protect them all orchards must be sprayed three or four times every summer with some fungicide. This spraying is now done by large power machines costing from $250 to $300, and if I am not mistaken the duty on them is thirty per cent. Hundreds of these machines are now in use in the valley, one firm last spring selling forty at a cost of $265 a piece.
But I could go on and write pages on what I consider the unfairness of the tariff laws as regards farmers and fruit-growers.
What is it worth a ton?

It ranges from $25 to $40 a ton; a good deal depends upon its quality. By reason of the change brought a/bout by the order of the Customs Board, an increased price per ton is now demanded of the farmers, and they are compelled to pay it.

Does my 'hon. friend give
the writer's name?

His name is Mt. Manning Ells, secretary of the Fruit Growers' Association of Nova Scotia, a gentleman who voluntarily wrote to me simply because I brought the matter to the notice of the House.
There are different ways of reducing the cost of living and helping the farmer, and I want to note the difference between the
methods adopted by Germany on the one hand and those adopted by Canada on the other. In Germany the government grants a rebate on freight paid on basic slag. In Canada freights are increased to the highest amount the goods can stand; that was done by the Intercolonial only a few months ago. In Germany Professor Wagner, Privy Councillor and Director of the Research Station said:
It would be exceedingly valuable if we could
secure a soluble basic phosphate, which we have seen almost equals superphosphate in its action, for the German market, but I do not believe that we can succeed in obtaining this, for, as far as I am informed, the high value of this slag has been recognized some time in England and the demand for it there must be already greater than the production.
We can, nevertheless, note as interesting to us, that Englishmen produce such an exceptionally quick and sure acting slag, and we must set our chemists and technical men to investigate, as far as possible, if the solubility of the Thomas slag obtained in the German works cannot, by some modification of the process be raised so as to equal that of the soluble basic phosphate.
In Canada, 10 per cent duty is imposed.
In England, the farmers agitate for a regulation to prohibit the exportation of basic slag, and their journal, the Mark Lane Express states:
It is a pity such good fertilizing material should leave the country.
In Canada, the cost is increased by imposing a duty and raising the freight rates.
Which, I ask you, is the more effective? This basic slag is of extreme importance to the people of eastern Canada, particularly to the horticulurists. I know that in Westmorland the farmers are very much agitated by reason of the (action of the Government in imposing this duty. They are placed at the mercy of one concern, a concern, taking their own representation, that has only $140,000 invested, and which does not give employment to very many men. That one concern, through its manager, can quietly and slyly approach the Government of Canada and secure, simply by an order of the Customs Board, a change in the tariff which imposes on eastern farmers and horticulturists an additional burden of at least $1.25 or $1.50 a ton.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the price has advanced that much this season?

I am so informed.
Mr. MORPHY. You vouch for that?

Yes, it is vouched for to me by very responsible people and by men who would have no object to serve in attempting to mislead me in the information. This -manager of one firm can come to

the Government and bring about such results; and yet the farmers, even although they come here by thousands, cannot have their wishes acceded to in the matter of free wheat. It shows a condition of things which should not prevail. That is one feature of the tariff that should have been remedied and I am surprised that the Finance 'Minister did not take it into consideration. He might have had 'brought to his notice the conditions which prevail. He was disposed to do something for the western farmers in the matter of a certain class of agricultural implements; but here is the secretary of this horticultural society stating that they have to pay thirty per cent on all the machinery necessary to be used in connection with their orchards. They are obliged, under the tariff as it stands, to pay a high duty imposed upon all the different classes of fertilizers that are brought into this country. These are a necessity for the farmer. Of what use is it for my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture to send his agents and officials from his Department all over the country to educate the farmer or to give grants to educational institutions and educational purposes in connection with agriculture, if he afterwards places burdens upon those who would wish to pat into execution the education which they secured by reason of his assistance? With the one hand he is giving some little assistance in the way of education, and with the other he is imposing barriers and obstacles in the way of those men utilizing successfully and profitably the education they have secured by reason of the grants made by the Government. I think it is a matter which my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture should bring home to the attention of the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the Government in order that this injustice may be remedied. I am not bringing this to the attention of the House merely as a political question. It is a business proposition which should have had the consideration of the Government and their supporters from the Maritime provinces at least. I am surprised that the members from the Annapolis valley, the hon. member from Annapolis county, the hon. member from the county of Kings and the hon. members from Digby and Hants, the citizens of all these counties are very largely interested in horticultural and other agricultural interests, have not urged this matter which is of deep import to their constituents. * There is another question which I would like to call particularly to the notice of the
Minister of Finance. A change was made in connection with this tariff schedule relating to building stone and it is a change that is very detrimental, in my judgment, to the quarrying interests of eastern, central and indeed of western Canada. It is a change that was made solely in the interests of the contractors on large public buildings throughout Canada, particularly those who are constructing large governmental buildings in this city and other cities

Is it no advantage to
the stone cutters?

-and not particularly, in my judgment, beneficial to the stone cutters, certainly not beneficial to any large percentage of them. My hon. friend must remember that there are thousands of stone cutters engaged in quarrying in Canada. The stone cutters who are employed in certain cities are not of the same number, and while it may benefit some particular men in that business it will not be of such great advantage to them as it will be to the contractors. This Government is condemned as a previous Government was condemned, because it has permitted, by the action of its architect, the use of Ohio and Indiana stone in the construction of public buildings built under the authority of Parliament.
That has been done everywhere. It is being done to a remarkable degree under this Government. It was being done by the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and there were complaints made to Parliament with respect to it a few years ago. The new station at Ottawa, built by the Grand Trunk, the Chateau Laurier and other buildings of a like character are examples. They were all built of Ohio and Ihdiana stone to the injury of the stone quarry interests of Canada. Here is a statement that was made on behalf of the Canadian building stone quarries. I will read it so that it may go on ' Hansard ':
The budget speech at Ottawa proposed to protect the stone cutting industry of Canada by increasing the duty on imported manufactured stone, making it fifteen cents per hundred pounds on stone sawn on four sides, and forty-five cents per hundred pounds on further manufactured stone. That will allow stone sawn on two sides (the only way in which it is imported as ' sawn stone ') to be brought in at the same rate as ' rough quarry blocks or practically free, and Is evidently worded in the interests of the contractors only, and it will be a great injury to Canadian quarries, as ' stone sawn on two sides' pays a higher duty under the old tariff. Most Canadian quarries are now provided with sawing machinery and can provide stones sawn oh

two sides or four sides, but contractors order it either in quarry blocks or sawn on two sides only. To ask for this change shows a very ungenerous disposition on the part of the contractors, as, they want high protection for the stone dressing industry but they want to import stone practically free of duty.
If allowed, this change will place the Canadian quarries completely at the mercy of the contractors. The country generally will be fully as favourable toward a moderate measure of protection to the quarrying industry, and the development of our great natural resources in this line, as to so heavily protecting the stone cutting business, working almost wholly on imported stone.
Canadian quarries should also share in this protection as suggested hereunder.
Rough rubble stone for rip-rap, breakwaters, etc., 5 cents per hundred pounds.
Rough blocks, not sawn or manufactured, 10 cents per hundred pounds.
Sawn on one or two sides, 20 cents per hundred pounds.
Further manufactured, 40 cents per hundred pounds.
Surely all members of Parliament, regardless of party, will favour the development of Canada's great natural wealth in stone. At present nearly all the building stone used in Canada is imported from the United States.
One reason for this preference is low freight rates from the quarries of Ohio and Indiana to the centres of population in Canada; another is that the imported stones are softer and cost less to cut and dress than the Canadian stone, but they are not nearly as strong and durable and give nothing like the warmth and wealth of colouring and texture the native stone offers. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick offer a great variety of sand stones and granites. Quebec has limestone, marble and granite. Ontario has sand stone, limestone and granite. Manitoba offers a particularly beautiful and durable limestone, and the great western provinces have rich sand stones, marbles and granites in great variety. One of our New Brunswick sandstones, tested at the McGill laboratories, was subjected to heat over 1,500 degrees F. for thirty minutes, plunged into cold water and then showed a crushing strength, of over 4,000 pounds per square inch, which is stronger than concrete. This stone, is similar in colour and texture to that used in the only building that went through the worst of the San Fransisco fire and is standing and occupied to-day, which shows that sand stones are as nearly fire proof as any material used. Canadian sand stones generally weigh more per cubic foot than the United States stones. The Ohio stones weigh 140 pounds per cubic foot and the Canadian sand stones average about 155 pounds, which, of course, makes them more durable but a little harder to cut. Heavy and expensive machinery is necessary to equip a quarry and usually a heavy outlay is necessary for rail connection, and some encouragement is necessary to warrant this expenditure in developing our natural building stone industry in the face of the great developments across the line. The fact "that the weekly or monthly outlay at quarries is nearly all for wages should be considered, as it shows that the percentage for wages is larger than usual.
That is one of the difficulties of protective tariffs. Here is a change made in the tariff with respect to building stone. By simply changing a few words und say-

ing that stone sawn on two sides shall come in practically on a free basis you give an advantage to the stone quarrymen of Ohio and to the contractors who are interested in patronizing the Ohio quarries.
My hon. friend is advocating protection.

I am not advocating it, but I say this is one of the difficulties of protection. You had a tariff which protected stone sawn on two sides, and which stone was subject to a certain duty. Now you change that and you place these other parties interested in the business at a very great disadvantage, and you simply favour the Government contractors and the few men whom they may employ in connection with the construction of buildings to the disadvantage of the money invested in the quarries of eastern, central and western Canada and to the detriment of the men engaged as quarrymen and stonecutters at these quarries. I have brought this to the notice of the House because the parties wrote to me in connection with it. I think that by tinkering in this way to suit certain particular interests you are not working to the advantage of the general interests of Canada.
I believe that every tariff should be framed in the open. Let there be light with respect to these matters. In the case of basic slag, the order which resulted in the imposition of taxation on the farmers of eastern Canada was passed in secret and by one man. Every business question comes back sooner or later to the question of the tariff. It cannot be avoided. Under our system we must have a tariff, but it should be framed in the open. I took occasion formerly to call attention to the dangers of Orders in Council and to the dangers incident to the passage of customs orders because it is all done in secret. The action taken by the former Government in consulting the people before framing the tariff of 1897 was commended at the time, and was worthy of commendation. It was an example that ought to have been followed by this Government. But that has not been done. In the case of the building stone question, had the matter been submitted to the quarry interests instead of to the contractors, a different result might have perhaps been secured. They had in the United States in the year 1828 a tariff which was known as a tariff of abomination. It was so called because it had no beginning, no end and no plan. It certainly had no traceable plan.

There was a general scramble, and everyone who had scrambled hard enough had to be taken care of in the schedule. Hence, it was not an equitable system, but it fully exemplified that definition of protection which characterized it as
at best an endless screw, and you never know when you have done with It. By protecting one industry you directly or indirectly hurt all others and have therefor to protect them too. By so doing you again damage the industry that you first protected and have to compensate it, but this compensation reacts as before on all other trades, and entitles them to redress, and so on ad infinitum.
The effect of protection in every country and upon every class is to weaken its will and narrow its enterprise; it teaches the classes to look outside of themselves. We have as a result the constant applications to the Government and to Parliament for endowments, and bonuses, and subsidies. We need not go outside of Canada for an illustration of this. It is equally evident in other countries, and particularly in high protectionist countries like Germany, where they have all kinds of bonuses, and where the German Government is kept constantly subsidizing and bonusing industries to the great detriment of the general interests of the country, and particularly the labouring classes. The so-called tariff of abominations in the United States had the merit of being a free-for-all, go-as-you-please kind of thing. But not so the course pursued by the Canadian Government, where special interests get their innings, and the great masses of the people are not consulted through their representatives even. The secret arangement system is injurious. It is devised in the interest of what we term the big interests; and I say nothing offensive of these big interests as long as they are made big by reason of their own competition and without stimulus in the nature of protection, or through combinations and trusts. These secret arrangements are generally the result of the influence exercised by the big interests. How many members of this House understand the changes made in the schedules of the tariff? We heard the Minister of Finance speaking of the changes in the steel schedule, and he told us the number of pounds to the yard, and that up to a certain number there would be a certain duty, and beyond a certain limit there would be a certain other duty; but who advised the Minister of Finance as to all this. No doubt the Minister of Finance has had the benefit
of the advice of those interested in that business, but the great consuming classes of Canada are not possessed of the technical knowledge which enables them to understand the effect of these changes. It would be against etiquette, I suppose, for the Minister of Finance to state who suggested these changes. Nowadays every expedient and device of secrecy is brought into use to keep the public unaware of the argument of high protectionists, ignorant of the facts which refute them, and uninformed of the intention of the promoters of protection. There is a will-o'-the-wisp known as the cost of production, which is accepted as a basis for tariffs, but it is elusive, changeable, and nowhere exists as a scientific demonstrable fact.
This country and the United States are familiar with the expert lobbyist whose business it is to deal with subjects of this kind, and they have been seen here for many years, but particularly are they in evidence during the present session, in anticipation of securing something in favour of this or that special interest. The Minister of Finance told us he had the benefit of information from the agricultural implement manufacturers, and he cited the cost of production, but he could not explain to the member for Assiniboia as to the watered stock. There has been a very marked change in the old order of things. There has been destruction of domestic competition by a combination of home rivals. The infant industry cry once prevailed, but the demands of to-day have far transcended that, and I shall not take up the time of the House to comment upon how far that idea has been transcended. It is argued by the interests that a young country wants protection in order to establish industries, and that an old country wants protection continued, because to lessen the protection would affect vested interests, and so: Protection once established, always established. Sometimes after the establishment of a protective tariff, there are symptoms of a desire for a change, by even those who created that tariff. That was well illustrated by the Conservative Government in 1894 when Sir John Thompson wanted to lop off the mouldering branches. Those who are the strongest in favour of a protective system realize that in the practical working of it an injustice is done here and there. Protection to be effective, to be what it is designed to be, namely, to shut out competition from other countries, should be widespread, and practically prohibitive. It is not; and the very fact that our tariff

to-day works inequalities and does injury here and there is recognized by everyone, even by those who favour the principle of protection. The hon. Minister of Finance openly avows his adherence to a policy of restriction and monopoly. Whiat is the present tariff policy of the hon. Minister of Finance as anmouinced by himself? It is a doctrine entirely new and different from that propounded toy Sir (Leonard Tilley in 1879. The new doctrine of the protectionist is that the tariff should represent the difference between the cost of production in Canada 'and the cost of production in other countries, plus a reasonable profit to those who axe engaged in the industry. The new part is ' plus a reasonable profit.' Who is to judge as to what that reasonable profit shall be? That policy openly guarantees profits to the men who come and ask favours of the Government. As a result of this, men, secure from foreign competition, have joined together in great combinations. They have felt the taste of blood and they want more. By reason of these combinations the cost of living has increased and complaints are heard from the mass of the people. Who has not heard of the cement trust? Even this Government heard of it and took action at a certain time to alleviate the damage that resulted. I have mentioned the other combinations. The industries of a certain Glass form a combination and, of course, each combination must have a compensation which will satisfy it and remove its competitors. The result is that the combination becomes enormous with a very large capitalization upon which dividends must be paid. Somebody must pay for these dividends, and that somebody is the consumer. While I am not in favour of protection., I say frankly and fairly that if you could have a moderate protection without the possibility of combines, many of the evils incident to protection would be eMminated. The great harm that has resulted is by reason of the combinations that have thus -been formed. When prices are falling, what do these combinations do? They reduce, hours of labour; they reduce production; they reduce wages; they throw men out of employment to do what? To keep the prices up in spite of their lack	of efficiency, that	has	beenthe	operation of trusts	and	combines in the United States and it is the operation and result of trusts and combines in Canada to-day. The great, evi1 of pro-
teotion is that it permits; it stimulates this result. We hear much of depression, of men out of employment, of slack-
11 p.m. of trade, of mills 'being closed down, and they are being closed down. In eastern Canada in the section of the country from which I come, in Nova Scotia during the past winter, the wages have been reduced, the number of employees lessened, and action taken, all in order that production may be lessened and prices kept up.
Is my hon. friend in favour of taking protection off cement now?

My hon. friend asks me if I am in favour of taking the protection off this thing or that thing. I say, you can not favour the one and discriminate against the other. If my hon. friend is in favour of withdrawing protection from everything, in the sense that it must he governed by a revenue tariff, I will heartily join with him in that true sense. There may have been a time when the tariff did not raise prices, but that time is past. That time has been taken advantage of by the great combines, to give them control of prices and wages. As has already .been stated toy my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lernieux), to those who demand free food, free wheat, and free agricultural implements, the answer is made that that means free trade. I *would like to ask the process of reasoning that would bring that about.
For election purposes.
How does it happen that agricultural implements are sold the cheapest to the farmers in countries that have-the highest protection?
I am not aware that that is the case.
It is the case.

If that be true, there may be many causes. What is the object of protection? It is to bring the level of prices up so that the manufacturers may toe able to manufacture at a profit as against the foreign manufacturers and the importation, of foreign goods? It must follow, as the night the day, that if you impose taxation for that purpose or for any other purpose, there must be an increase of the cost of that particular article.
Mr. BLAIN; I say not.

When you buy an imported article you pay part of the price into the revenue of the Dominion in the form of customs duty; hut as a rule what you buy-

is not the imported ibut the domestic article, the price of which the manufacturer has been able to raise to a point equal to or higher than the price of the foreign article plus the duty. I think that is an axiomatic statement. Who gets the tax then? Not the Government surely, but the manufacturer.
The wage earner gets the advantage.
My hon. friend had better confine himself to the Hindu. The idea to which he gives expression that protection increases wages has become absurd beyond the, point of absurdity.
It can be demonstrated.

It can be demonstrated that the hon. gentleman is entirely wrong. However, I will listen to him, when he speaks, with close attention and all patience. It is a confession of the inability of the Canadian, manufacturer to compete for him to ask for these privileges. We are asked to pay him a price from 15 per cent to 35 per cent or more higher than we pay the foreign manufacturer. That is how this colossal infant, this bearded infant, treats the people to-day. He started out with the idea that he should be protected in his infancy, but now after many years he is apparently the same infant, feeding from the same nursing-bottle. Such a policy has become the means of fostering the growth of a number of groups of industries at the expense of the economic vitality of the country. This idea was very splendidly expressed by Mr. Woodrow Wilson in his appeals to the American people before the last presidential election.
The Liberal party constitutes practically half the population of Canada, and yet these people are being denounced as disloyal because they advocate a reduction of taxation, because they favour a policy which means free food to the people and free raw material to the agriculturists. I think it might well be said that, being half the population and engaged in all classes of enterprises, they must have the same interest in the prosperity of the country as have those who favour a different policy. One writer, speaking of these people, says that they cannot commit economic murder without committing economic suicide. As a party, we do not propose to destroy the foundation of our own economic structure. One very foolish writer actually
said that the policy of free food and the reduction of taxation ' will blast the bedrock of our national prosperity Was a more absurd statement than that ever written?
We used to hear a good deal about the slaughter market. When it was proposed to have a heavy duty on boots and shoes, it was said we must have such a duty because unless the Canadian manufacturer has the protection, the country will be invaded by the American manufacturer who will slaughter this market while he enjoys the benefit of protection in his own market by reason of the high tariff of the United States. That cry does not apply to-day. The United States admits free the boots and shoes manufactured in Canada. As a matter of fact, Canadian shoe manufacturers are to-day exploiting the markets of the United States, and doing it successfully, in competition with their American rivals. Upon what principle, I ask, should they claim a monopoly of the Canadian market when the American market is open to them?
How many have allowed themselves for so long to be imposed upon by the claim that the protective tariff is for the benefit of the workingman in the presence of so many facts to the contrary? The audacity, the impudence of the claim is what amazes one in the face of the fact that the workingmen of this country who are in unprotected industries are better paid than those who are in protected industries. I am free to admit that there cannot be free trade-(I wish in all interests there could be)-so long as the indirect instead of the direct method of taxation prevails as arranged at the dawn of Confederation. But we can ameliorate wrongs, remove burdens, restrict special privileges, curb big interests, nourish freedom and liberty and sever the bonds of the masses. We can crush out the processes of favouritism granted at the expense of the masses. We can destroy the weeds to give room and air and light to nourish the plant so essential to the lives of our great consuming population, the toiling masses, that they may grow and thrive to the status of a prosperous, contented and happy people.- Lop the mouldering branches? Aye, and cut and dig up the dead root of privilege which bars nutriment from the other the life-giving roots. In the words of a great tariff reformer:
The policy of freeing the country from a restricted tariff will so variegate and multiply the undertakings in the country that there will be a wider market and a greater competition for labour; it will let the sun shine through the clouds again as once it shone on the free,

independent, unpatronized intelligence of a great people.
Industries have become cowardly and. dependent upon Government aid. Apparently a curse is upon them as witness the constant applications to the Government for additional privileges.
' We should make our tariffs not like those who dole out favours, but like those who serve a nation,' were the words of a great man, and I commend them to the consideration of this House and of the people of Canada, whose interests we are called upon to safeguard.

Mr. Speaker, in rising for the first time to ask the attention of this House, it is but natural that I should feel that hesitation and, perhaps, nervousness, that is common to most persons who occupy a position similar to- the one which I occupy to-night. However, I do not intend to go into the matters under debate at any great length, as I do not wish to inflict upon the House everything that I would have to say with regard to them. The question that is before the House has been discussed by some of the best minds that our country produces, and I do not think that any remarks which I may add to theirs will educate the members of this House or the people of the country. I will simply content myself with giving a few humble opinions as to the facts and principles laid down by the Minister of Finance in his Budget speech.
In the first place, I wish to convey to the Minister of Finance not only my own congratulations, but also the congratulations of a number of my most intelligent electors who have read his speech and are convinced that we have to-day at the head of affairs men who are willing and anxious to legislate according to the requirements of our country. There are in my county electors as intelligent, perhaps, as there are in the majority of rural districts and I have it direct from them that they have absolute confidence in the future of Canada when its affairs are conducted by such men as we have in the persons of our Prime Minister and the members of his Cabinet.
Mr. Speaker, I represent a rural constituency, and I have heard so much about the farmers since I came here that I have reason to be proud that I represent a rural constituency. The conditions in my county are very different from what they are in the rural constituencies about which we have heard so much in the course of this debate.	As you all know,

I have the honour to represent the county of Chateauguay, and I do not think I am saying too much when I say that that county ranks among the foremost in the province of Quebec, perhaps in the whole Dominion. There was a time when the people of that county were not in the prosperous condition that they are in to-day. It is within my own recollection, Sir, when the people of that county were selling their produce for less than it cost them to produce it. I have seen the time when the people in the county of Chateauguay were selling their hay for less than it really cost them to harvest it.
That was before 1896.

Not fifteen years ago,
when the late Government was in power, those conditions prevailed in the county which I represent. I am proud to say that the electors of Chateauguay did not go begging to this or to any other Government. They got down to work; they plodded, and to-day they occupy a position that to me and to them is an honourable one. How have they done it? What has brought that about? They simply waited quietly until the policy laid down by the Conservative party would have its due and proper effect. They realized that great bodies move slowly, and that it would take time for that policy to have the effects which we are feeling to-day, and which, as our friends opposite know, do exist at the present time.	These effects can be .
attributed to the beneficial operation of a protective policy. To-day those men realize that they owe their present condition to the policy of the Conservative party, under the exercise of which we have built up a home market. We have near us today the great market of Montreal, which is equal if not in advance of any in this great Dominion. We realize that had we not followed the policy that was laid down in 1879 by the Conservative party, that city would not be the city that it is today, and the farmers of my county would not have the market at their door which they have at the present time. The farmers of my locality understand that many products cannot be shipped abroad, and they have the market for those products at their very door. I feel satisfied in saying that they give credit to the Conservative party for having brought about those conditions.
From the arguments to which we have listened for the last couple of days, one

would almost be led to think that there was but one class of people in this country worthy of the consideration of this House, that is the farmers of the West. I have a fellow feeling with the farmers, I am a farmer myself; but I am of the impression that there is a number of so-called farmers in our western country, perhaps a large percentage of the wheat growers of the West, who do not merit the title of farmer. It is my impression, although I have never been there and speak only from what I have been fold by men of experience, that a large percentage of the wheat growers of the West are not farmers at all but simply men who are exploiting our feitile western land. In due course of time the actual farmer will have to go in and build up, by a proper system of farming, the lands that are today being depleted or exhausted by a continuation of the one crop. For that reason I say that we are perhaps giving too much attention to what are called the farmers of the West. As I have said there are people in this country engaged in the business of farming. They have my sympathy, they should have the support and I am satisfied will have the support of this Government; but I maintain that the agitation that has been made before this House is not on behalf of the actual farmers but is in the interests of men who are exploiting our fertile fields of the Northwest. For that reason I think that it behooves this Government to be careful as to how they deal with this question of free wheat. In the early part of this session an hon. member read a paper on the floor of this House stating that the Canadian producers, or in other words the Canadian flour, was successfully competing in the markets of China with the products of our American neighbours. To my mind that gives a clue to the very great desire that our neighbours to the south have to get pur wheat. What will be the result to the farmers of our western country? Our American neighbours are a far-sighted people. We know tnat from the fact that two years ago they offered us reciprocity. Fortunately the people of Canada were wise enough to see through that offer and were not ready to become an adjunct of the United States.
It appears to me that we would be doing an injury to the farmers of the West if we should allow our No. 1 hard wheat to go into the mills of the United States. The object is plain to me, they wish simply to raise the standard of their flour and eventually drive the Canadian competitor out of the foreign market. For that reason I would 170
strongly urge this Government to be careful in regard to the question of free wheat. We have heard so much about that question and men have entertained such extreme views on it that I shall not pursue it further.
Anothecc question that has not been dealt with to the same extent as I expected it would have been, is the rapid increase in the price of beef on the American side of the line. When I speak along this line I speak from actual knowledge and experience. As you know, the Montreal and Dundee railway Turns through my county almost from one end to the other and runs pretty nearly parallel with the provincial boundary. I know for a fact that three years ago the bulk of the beef cattle that were taken to the market of Montreal were smuggled into this country from the state of New York and sent to Montreal by the railroad that I have spoken of. In one year's time what has brought about the changed condition of affairs? That question is more than I can solve, but it certainly was not a natural growth. The rapid increase in the price of beef was due to some cause that does not appear on the surface, certainly not a natural growth. I believe it has its sequel in the movement of troops and warships that has been taking place in the last few days into Mexican waters. It is my conviction that the almost unreasonable demand for beef cattle in this country arose from the demand for naval and military supplies. They were taken up regardless of quality, regardless of condition, regardless of disease. I know for a fact that we had diseased cattle in our community that were taken and we were told they were for canning purposes. I am firmly of the conviction that the movement of troops down into Mexican waters is the cause of the great demand for our beef for export to the United States; it was required to prepare our American neighbours for what will possibly take place within the next few mouths.
With regard to the high cost of living, I have only to say that I marvel at some of the arguments that have been adduced. I do not think that we have yet had any arguments advanced that prove to us that this or any other Government could solve that problem. In my opinion they will simply have to do as the farmers do in my county; that is they will have to wait until the conditions change, for then only can a satisfactory solution be arrived at.



It cannot be done by this Government. We are told that the tariff is the cause of the high cost of living. Who are the people who are suffering the most? We hear a great many complaints on behalf of the farmers, but in my opinion it is the labouring classes who are suffering the most from the high cost of living. How could we relieve that situation by abolishing the tariff? These labouring men are dependent upon the factories in our land for their living. Reduce or take off the duties imposed by the tariff now in existence and what will be the result ? What would the men who are suffering do ? We would have those charitable institutions and bread lines which have been spoken of in Montreal, before next spring. I trust that with the wisdom of the men who are to day at the head of affairs, these questions will regulate themselves and will, in due course of time, be solved.
